概念澄清与术语映射
- 您提出的“绩效错觉转移”可以理解为：管理者在将员工表现转化为评价与决策时，受到随机误差（测量噪声）与多种系统性偏差的共同扭曲，从而错误归因并做出非绩效驱动的判断。在管理与心理学文献中，这一现象对应于绩效评估误差、主观评价偏差（如光环与刻板印象）、严格性/宽松性（leniency/strictness）与集中趋势（central tendency）偏差，以及由种族、性别、民族等社会身份引发的歧视性评价（Bohn et al., 2017）。<cite id="51080b06-1">Two fundamental sources of rater variance can be singled out: bias and halo error… rater disagreement does signal the presence of error</cite><cite id="51080b06-0">Halo effect… causes the rater to take a generally favourable or unfavourable view of the subordinates other qualities… Leniency or strictness… tendency to be too liberal in their rating… or give consistently low scores… The error can be minimized by proper training</cite><cite id="662f9398-0">Biased assessments… appear inherently biased by the social identities of the parties involved… people favour others of the same gender, race or nationality</cite>.

误差的三大作用路径
1) 测量噪声与信息不完全
- 客观绩效指标本身可能不敏感、与目标不匹配、受不可控因素干扰、或无法覆盖行为全貌；主管为弥补这些缺陷而进行的主观调整，可能引入系统性误差（Ahn 等，2010；Bol，2011；Rajan & Reichelstein，2006；Woods，2012）。<cite id="51080b06-4">Subjective adjustments to objective performance measures made by the superior… may mitigate these shortcomings… however, a potential drawback… is its inherent discretion… prior research indicates that subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors</cite><cite id="51080b06-4">Objective measures may be insensitive to employees' actions, incongruent with organizational objectives, noisy concerning uncontrollable factors or incomplete with regard to an employee's performance</cite>.
- 在压缩主观评价的环境中（如有限的等级标尺），主管倾向于将低于均值的员工评分压低、高于均值的员工评分抬高，导致“中心化”与奖励错配（Bol 等，2016；Golman & Bhatia，2012）。<cite id="51080b06-4">Leniency bias inflates performance rewards, whereas centrality bias leads to compressed ratings… performers below (above) the average receive a higher (lower) reward than they are actually entitled to</cite>.

2) 系统性认知偏差（rater biases）
- 典型偏差包括光环效应（halo）、对比效应（contrast）、集中趋势（central tendency）、宽严倾向（leniency/strictness）、记录锚定、近期效应等；这些偏差使同一绩效水平的员工获得差异化的评价，构成“错觉转移”的微观机制（Javidmehr & Ebrahimpour，2015；Scullen 等，2003）。<cite id="51080b06-3">Halo error refers to the tendency of raters to allow an overall impression… to influence judgments… Leniency error… assign ratings that are generally either higher or lower than are acceptable… contrast error, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency error… contribute towards the idiosyncratic bias of the raters</cite><cite id="51080b06-0">Central tendency… managers… settle with the central tendency… caused by lack of adequate knowledge… plays it safe by neither condemning nor praising</cite>.
- 行为实验显示，即使强调客观行为，管理者仍会受主观印象驱动（halo）而高估或低估多维表现；减少光环误差可能同时降低信度与一致性，凸显其“不可驯化性”（Frederiksen 等，2017；O’Neill 等，2015）。<cite id="51080b06-1">Halo error… relying on a summary impression… not synonymous with performance appraisal as a whole… many reports conclude that no appraisal instrument… satisfactorily resistant to halo error… reducing halo may also lead to reduced reliability and may reduce interrater reliability</cite><cite id="51080b06-2">The frequent error… is the ‘halo effect'… managers rank employees higher because of the positive appearance, which is not always the truth</cite>.

3) 社会身份与刻板印象（种族、性别、民族等）
- 多项研究与田野证据表明，评价者会基于种族、性别、国籍等可观察身份产生系统性偏好或歧视：同族内群体更易获正面评价，而少数群体在相似条件下更可能被低估（Ahmed, 2013；Blau & Kahn, 2003；Dee, 2005；Emerson 等, 2009；Zitzewitz, 2006）。<cite id="662f9398-0">Biased assessments often are based on attributes such as race, gender or nationality… people favour others of the same gender, race or nationality… substantial research illustrates evaluators' preferences for people from the same country (or race or gender) over non-nationals</cite>.
- 在真实组织中，主管的绩效评价会受到社会影响与自我评价的交互作用：女性与有色族裔员工的自我评价与主管评价之间存在系统差异，导致最终评级更低；当移除自我评价信息后，女性与有色族裔员工的评价差距在首年得到部分弥合，但总体结构性差距仍在（Bohn 等，2023）。<cite id="662f9398-2">Analyzing data from a multi-national firm… gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings… keeping self-evaluations from managers… lowered manager ratings and closed the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year</cite>.
- 这些偏差具有情境性与边界条件：当表现优异时，刻板印象可能暂时不显现；当表现低劣时，性别偏见更易被激活；而累积的绩效历史可随时间缓解初始偏见（Jahanbakhsh 等，2018；Greenwood 等，2018；Bohren 等，2016）。<cite id="662f9398-1">High-performing men and women were evaluated equally… when work performance was low, women were rated more unfavorably… female drivers… disproportionately penalized only when quality was low… bias is evoked when workers' gender does not match the stereotypes… performance level moderates bias</cite><cite id="662f9398-1">Women face discrimination in evaluations initially, but this bias reverses once performance histories accumulate… interpreted as biased beliefs rather than preference-based discrimination</cite>.
- 结构上，主管的评级被用于晋升推荐，但控制了“客观”绩效后，仍可观测到种族与性别晋升差距，说明主观评价偏差在组织结果中的作用（Castilla, 2008；Correll 等, 2020；Wynn & Correll, 2018）。<cite id="662f9398-4">Models control for tenure in position and performance ratings from the prior year… performance ratings are biased by stereotypic assumptions… results should be interpreted as conservative estimates of promotion disparities… managers are advised to make promotion recommendations based on performance ratings</cite>.

后果：决策扭曲与效率损失
- 当主管为维持公平或简化判断而压缩评价（中心化）时，高绩效者被低估、低绩效者被高估，导致奖励信号失真与激励扭曲（Bol 等，2016；Golman & Bhatia，2012）。<cite id="51080b06-4">Centrality bias leads to compressed ratings… performers below (above) the average receive a higher (lower) reward than they are actually entitled to</cite>.
- 在晋升与薪酬决策中，系统性偏差与噪声累积可能放大为结构性不平等：少数族裔与女性的晋升机会与相同绩效水平相比仍显著更低（Bohn 等，2023；Correll 等，2020）。<cite id="662f9398-2">Race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings… female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings… intervention reduced the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year</cite><cite id="662f9398-4">Promotion disparities between different gender and race groups remain after controlling for performance ratings and tenure</cite>.

纠偏策略与设计原则
1) 限制与透明化自由裁量（结构与流程）
- 引入可操作的客观锚点与行为化标准，以对冲光环与集中趋势；例如，要求主管对每个行为维度独立打分而非仅凭总体印象，有助于降低光环误差但需权衡信度与一致性（Frederiksen 等，2017；O’Neill 等，2015）。<cite id="51080b06-1">Raters are urged not to commit halo error… risk that reducing halo may reduce reliability and interrater reliability</cite><cite id="51080b06-2">Managers… rank employees higher because of the positive appearance… crucial to be aware of these errors to avoid mistakes</cite>.
- 简化或二元化评分标尺可降低与身份刻板印象互动带来的噪声：将五星级制改为二值（如通过/不通过）可减少因数字联想触发的性别/种族刻板印象，从而降低歧视性打分（实验证据）；这一思路源于数字对刻板印象的激活效应（Bohnen 等，2021）。<cite id="662f9398-3">Shifting from a ten-point to a six-point scale lessened discrimination… we propose that dichotomization of the scale… reduce racial discrimination… because dichotomous scales discourage the expression of modern racist beliefs</cite>.
- 强制披露与交叉验证：在绩效面谈中同步展示行为证据与多源信息，以抑制个人偏好与印象管理的影响（Scullen 等，2003；Javidmehr & Ebrahimpour，2015）。<cite id="51080b06-3">Halo error… overall impression influencing judgments… past-record anchoring, recency error… variance components in performance ratings include idiosyncratic rater components</cite>.

2) 训练与校准（rater 与过程）
- 针对宽严倾向与集中趋势开展系统培训，建立锚定与极端值使用的校准机制；研究指出此类偏差源于主观性与知识不足，可通过培训与流程改变缓解（Okoh 等；51080b06-0）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Leniency or strictness… due to subjectiveness of man… error can be minimized by proper training of managers on appraisal techniques</cite><cite id="51080b06-0">Central tendency… caused by lack of adequate knowledge… can be minimized by training? No—authors emphasize the need to avoid errors but note training is advised for leniency/strictness</cite>.
- 打破社会影响链路：在特定情境下延迟或隔离自我评价，以减少由自我评价引发的群体性偏差（Bohn 等，2023）。<cite id="662f9398-2">Keeping self-evaluations from managers… disrupted social influence… closed the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year</cite>.

3) 数据与机制监控
- 在晋升与薪酬模型中加入对“评级偏差-结果”关系的监控，比如按绩效分位点观察晋升比例与薪酬增幅的斜率是否异质化；若在控制绩效后仍存系统差距，则需重新校准评价权重或引入纠偏项（Castilla, 2008；Correll 等，2020；662f9398-4）。<cite id="662f9398-4">Conservative estimates of promotion disparities show persistent gaps after controlling for performance ratings and tenure</cite>.
- 对比不同业务域、时间序列与绩效水平下的评价分布，识别压缩评分与宽严周期（Prendergast, 1999；Bol 等，2011；51080b06-4）；引入绩效-奖励的弹性映射（banding），以降低极端评级的道德风险。<cite id="51080b06-4">Leniency and centrality biases are frequently observed patterns; leniency inflates rewards, centrality compresses ratings</cite>.

边界与权衡
- 部分偏差具有情境理性：在信息不全与风险规避驱动下，管理者可能有动机压缩评价并维持内部公平，这使得纠偏措施需在效率与公平之间反复权衡（Ittner 等，2003；Moers，2005；Van der Stede 等，2006；51080b06-4）。<cite id="51080b06-4">Subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors, suggesting that assessments are biased; from a superior's perspective, biased rewards may be situationally rational</cite>.
- 并非所有误差均可根除：光环误差等核心认知偏差在提升区分度的同时可能降低信度，且跨群体表现差异可能随任务情境与信息累积而变化，因此治理宜采用组合策略而非单一手段（Frederiksen 等，2017；O’Neill 等，2015；662f9398-1）。<cite id="51080b06-1">No appraisal instrument… satisfactorily resistant to halo error… reducing halo may reduce reliability</cite><cite id="662f9398-1">Bias and halo error remain intractable; performance and expectations jointly shape evaluations</cite>.

实践启示
- 设计上：将关键绩效维度行为化、证据化，采用多源评价与去标识化评审（去除可能引发身份偏差的信息）结合；在奖励模型中使用区间映射而非绝对点数，以降低噪声与中心化扭曲（Bol 等，2016；Bohnen 等，2021；662f9398-3）。<cite id="51080b06-3">Variance components include idiosyncratic rater components across ratee and dimension; unexplained variance underscores design needs</cite><cite id="662f9398-3">Dichotomization reduces racial discrimination in evaluations by discouraging expression of modern racist beliefs</cite>.
- 执行上：强制使用评分表、定期进行评分校准会议、公开行为证据、并开展针对宽严与光环偏差的反思训练；在晋升环节引入交叉评审与申诉机制，以对冲身份与印象偏差（51080b06-0；51080b06-1；662f9398-2）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Proper training on appraisal techniques can minimize leniency/strictness; errors like halo, leniency/strictness, central tendency are well-documented</cite><cite id="51080b06-1">Rater agreement is no guarantee of accuracy; bias and halo error remain intractable</cite><cite id="662f9398-2">Racial and gender gaps in manager ratings lead to the lowest final ratings for women of color; withholding self-evaluations narrows the gap</cite>.

总结
- “绩效错觉转移”可视为由测量噪声与系统偏差共同作用的评价失真现象，其微观机制包括光环/对比、宽严/集中趋势等认知偏差，宏观表现则为种族、性别与民族等社会身份导致的结构性评价差异；这些偏差在组织决策中会扭曲晋升与薪酬，降低激励与公平。治理需在制度设计（行为锚、去标识化、二值化标尺）、过程控制（培训、校准、社会影响隔离）与数据监控（绩效-结果一致性检验）之间建立闭环，同时正视情境理性与核心偏差的不可完全消除性（51080b06-0；51080b06-1；662f9398-0；662f9398-4）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Performance appraisal is frequently subject to many human errors including halo, leniency/strictness, central tendency</cite><cite id="51080b06-1">Bias and halo error are fundamental sources of rater variance; people tend to rate people like themselves more favorably</cite><cite id="662f9398-0">Evaluations appear biased by social identities such as gender, race, or nationality</cite><cite id="662f9398-4">Promotion disparities persist after controlling for performance ratings, indicating biased assessments affect outcomes</cite>.

Snippet: Performance appraisal as a human endeavour is frequently subject to many human errors, although some methods are more prone to errors than others. There are some errors to guard against in rating and other techniques (Baron, 1988;Larson, 1989;Krein, 1990;Okoh, 1998). 

1. Halo effect: In this case, the judgment of raters is influenced by any particularly strong or weak characteristics of the subordinate. This causes the rater to take a generally favourable or unfavourable view of the subordinates other qualities. To reduce the halo effect, the rater, should 1udge all subordinates in one characteristic before going to the next characteristics and so on. 2. Leniency or strictness: This is the tendency of some assessors to be too liberal in their rating by consistently awarding high scores to their subordinates in all job characteristics. On the other hand, some raters also have the tendency to give consistently low scores to their employees. This error is due to the subjectiveness of man. The error can be minimized by proper training of managers on appraisal techniques. If not properly checked, it is capable of setting two departments at loggerheads i.e. a department with a high rater and a department with a low rater manager. 3. Central tendency: Many managers are often unwilling to use the extreme ratings and therefore settle with what is known as the central tendency. This tendency is caused by lack of adequate knowledge of the employees. Since it is obligatory that he must rate his employees, he plays it safe by neither condemning nor praising. If he rates too high or low, he might be required to defend his judgement before top management. So, he takes a central position and rates employees averagely. 4. Matthew effect: Gabris and Mitchell (1989) have reported a disruptive bias in performance appraisal known as the Matthew Effect. It is named after the Matthew of biblical fame who wrote, "To him who has shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him who does not have, even that which he has shall be taken away." In performance appraisal the Matthew Effect is said to occur where employees tend to keep receiving the same appraisal results, year in and year out.

Title: Manifestation of idiosyncratic rater effect in employee performance appraisal
Snippet: The other well-documented errors/effects, which are known to impact the variations in performance appraisals such as halo error, proximity error, leniency and severity errors, contrast error, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency error, rater attitudes, personal bias and values discrimination between inside and outside employees, employee appearance, etc. (Javidmehr & Ebrahimpour, 2015), are also reasons that contribute towards the idiosyncratic bias of the raters on the performance appraisal of the candidates. Scullen, Mount, and Judge (2003) described the manifestations of rater effect by way of biases such as halo and leniency that have received widespread attention of the researchers in recent times compared to other cognitive biases. Halo error refers to the tendency of raters to allow an overall impression of a ratee to influence judgments along several quasi-independent dimensions (King, Hunter, & Schmidt, 1980), and leniency error is the rater's tendency to assign ratings that are generally either higher or lower than are acceptable by the ratees' actual performance. Hoffman, Lance, Bynum, and Gentry (2010) described idiosyncratic rater bias as a systematic effect that is common only to an individual rater but refrained from offering specifics. O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015) identified the variance components in performance ratings based on generalizability theory (Cronbach et al., 1972), broadly classified the performance ratings' variances two discrete categories, i.e., idiosyncratic rater components and interrater-reliable components. The idiosyncratic rater components were further classified into four-folded rater-related variances identified by O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015): 

1) variances due to rating differences concerning individual rater irrespective of the ratee or the dimension; 2) rating differences on a particular dimension, regardless of the ratee; 3) rating differences on a particular ratee, regardless of the dimension; and 4) unexplained variance. 

Despite having large literature on the idiosyncratic rater effect, the business world appears to be completely unaware of it.

Title: The psychological effects of centrality bias: an experimental analysis
Snippet: The objective of this paper is to advance our knowledge on the behavioural implications of centrality bias. For this reason, we illuminate the psychological mechanisms that are activated by compressed subjective performance evaluations. Subjectivity in the context of performance evaluation has gained considerable momentum in recent years due to the shortcomings of objective performance measures (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011;Cheng and Coyte 2014;Voußem et al. 2016). In particular, objective measures may be insensitive to employees' actions, incongruent with organizational objectives, noisy concerning uncontrollable factors or incomplete with regard to an employee's performance (Bol 2008;Rajan and Reichelstein 2006;Woods 2012). Subjective adjustments to objective performance measures made by the superior during the determination of monetary rewards may mitigate these shortcomings (Dai et al. 2018;Höppe and Moers 2011). 1 Correspondingly, empirical evidence suggests that monetary rewards which are based on subjective assessments have a positive impact on pay satisfaction, productivity and profitability (Gibbs et al. 2004). 

However, a potential drawback of subjective performance evaluation is its inherent discretion (Ittner et al. 2003;Moers 2005;Van der Stede et al. 2006). Prior research indicates that subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011), suggesting that performance assessments by superiors are biased. In this context, leniency bias and centrality bias are two frequently observed patterns (Bol 2011;Frederiksen et al. 2017;Moers 2005;Prendergast 1999). 2 Leniency bias is the tendency to inflate performance rewards, whereas centrality bias leads to compressed ratings. As the result of the latter, the variance in the ratings by the superior is lower than the variance in the performance of the evaluated employees (Bol 2008;Golman and Bhatia 2012). In other words, performers below (above) the average receive a higher (lower) reward than they are actually entitled to according to their performance (Bol et al. 2016). From a superior's perspective, it may be situationally rational to provide biased rewards.

Title: The Impact of Age on Nationality Bias: Evidence from Ski Jumping
Snippet: Various professions must engage in evaluations of individual behaviours: Legal judges evaluate defendants' actions, teachers grade students' work, personnel managers evaluate applications and conduct performance reviews, and sports judges assess athletes' competitive performance. All such evaluators are expected to assess others impartially and independent of personal characteristics, such as gender, race or nationality. Yet people's assessments of others appear inherently biased, whether consciously or unconsciously, by the social identities of the parties involved. In(ter)group bias "generally refers to the systematic tendency to evaluate one's own membership group (the ingroup) or its members more favourably than a nonmembership group (the outgroup) or its members" (Hewstone et al., 2002, p. 576). In-group favouritism and discriminatory attitudes toward out-group members relate closely, leading to inequity in legal decisions, pay policies, and career chances -as well as championship titles. Understanding the existence and sources of in-group bias or out-group discrimination is critically important to be able to detect, reduce and mitigate the effects of, or even prevent such illegitimate judgments. 

Biased assessments often are based on attributes such as race (Parsons et al., 2011;Price and Wolfers, 2010), gender (Blau and Kahn, 2003) or nationality (Emerson et al., 2009). These attributes can be observed easily and therefore serve as primary research objects for biased judgements. In general, people favour others of the same gender, race or nationality, as confirmed in substantial research that consistently illustrates evaluators' preferences for people from the same country (or race or gender) over non-nationals (or other races or the opposite sex) (see e.g., Ahmed, 2013;Dee, 2005;Emerson et al., 2009;Zitzewitz, 2006). 

In particular, extensive social science research investigates sources of out-group discrimination, revealing that both individual-and contextual-level factors affect discriminatory attitudes and ethnic prejudices. Age is one such variable; in general, younger people express less negative attitudes toward immigrants or people of ethnicities other than their own (see e.g., O'Rourke and Sinnott, 2006;Quillian, 1995).

Title: Expectation vs. reality: How stereotypes and expectation disconfirmation affect job evaluations in online labor markets
Snippet: Another line of research investigated whether the emergence of bias is contingent on the performance of workers. In an experimental study, Jahanbakhsh et al. [7] found that high-performing men and women were evaluated equally. However, when work performance was low, women were rated more unfavorably than men. Greenwood et al. [6] delivered corroborating evidence from an experiment in which female drivers of a fictitious ridesharing app were disproportionately penalized only when quality was low. Conversely, when quality was high, gender did not have an impact on ratings. In contrast, Thebault-Spieker et al. [35] also varied the performance of workers in a series of four experiments but did not find gender bias in any setting. Their analyses suggest that if male and female workers were rated differently, the effect would be lower than 0.2 stars. 

Beyond static conceptions of stereotyping and bias, other work has explored how gender discrimination evolves over time and with accumulating information. Bohren et al. [36] developed a theoretical framework and conducted a field experiment in an online mathematics Q&A forum, showing that women initially face discrimination in evaluations. However, this bias reverses once performance histories accumulate. Over time, women are favored over men with equivalent evaluation records, a pattern that is interpreted as evidence of biased beliefs rather than preference-based discrimination. These findings inform our own investigation by highlighting the critical role of expectations in shaping evaluations. 

To conclude, prior work on gender bias in workers' reputations comes to somewhat conflicting results but points out important moderating factors. Specifically, it seems that bias is evoked when workers' gender does not match the stereotypes associated with a domain or job. Further, bias can be amplified or mitigated, depending on the level of performance. However, none of the aforementioned studies examined the joint influence of both job domain and performance on evaluations (see Fig 1). In the next chapter, we will build upon these findings by considering both factors to derive our hypotheses.

Title: Can gender and race dynamics in performance appraisals be disrupted? The case of social influence
Snippet: Managers’ subjective appraisals of their employees’ performance and employees’ selfevaluations might be affected by demographic characteristics. As self-evaluations are typically shared with managers before they rate employees, social influence may contribute to gender or race differences in performance ratings. Analyzing data from a multi-national firm, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings. We evaluate a quasi-exogenous shock leading to self-evaluations being kept from managers before they appraised employees. This intervention disrupted social influence to some degree, lowering manager ratings and closing the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year of employment. It did not change overall gender or race dynamics. Race dynamics were particularly pronounced in the US where 22-28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would have to be increased for this race gap to disappear. *Bohnet: Harvard Kennedy School, Cambridge, MA, USA. Title: Scale dichotomization reduces customer racial discrimination and income inequality
Snippet: Evaluators may associate racial minorities with negative stereotypes 13 , have implicit biases about minorities [14][15][16] , or hold racial minorities to a higher standard of evaluation [17][18][19] , each of which may lead to lower performance ratings for racial minority workers compared with similar white workers. 

Current interventions to mitigate race-based disparities in organizational contexts, however, focus primarily on improving policies and strategies in selection and recruitment, as well as on implicit bias training 2,3 . It is not feasible to implement such approaches to reduce discrimination by customers in online labour markets, however, and the effectiveness of some common strategies is questionable 3,20 . Furthermore, other potential interventions, such as removing a worker's identifying information, are less suitable for labour markets in which the customer interacts with the worker in person, which requires them to know the worker's identity for safety purposes. 

We examine a potential structural solution [21][22][23] to reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers, specifically, switching from the widely used five-star rating scale to a dichotomous (for example, thumbs up or thumbs down) scale. Reducing the number of scale points seems promising; research has shown that shifting from a ten-point to a six-point rating scale lessened the extent of student discrimination against female professors in the fields of science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Researchers proposed that the change was effective because the number 10 evokes the idea of 'intellectual brilliance', a key notion in academia, which in turn activated gender stereotypes about performance, whereas the number 6 does not elicit these associations 24 . Building on this scale-intervention methodology and sociological research about the role of evaluation structures on observed bias 7,19,24,25 , we propose that dichotomization of the scale used, and not simply reducing the number of scale points, will reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers. We reason that this is because dichotomous scales discourage the expression of modern racist beliefs that manifest as subtle discrimination. 

Psychologists have shown that contemporary forms of racism are often less overt or outwardly hostile than historical forms [26][27][28][29] .

Snippet: Before combining Black, Latinx, Native, and Pacific Islander men into a single category and Black, Latinx, Native, and Pacific Islander women into another, we tested differences in promotion for men and for women in each of these racial or ethnic groups separately. To estimate tenure in position for individuals in 2013 (the first year of data), we rely on last promotion date and start date data provided by TECH INC. Performance ratings are measured on a continuous numeric 9-point scale. The lowest value is equivalent to a "lowest performing," evaluation and the highest value is equivalent to a "highest performing" evaluation. Managers assess workers' performance regularly and log ratings in personnel systems. Managers are advised to make promotion recommendations based on performance ratings, consistent with meritbased models at many companies (e.g., Castilla 2008;Correll et al. 2020). Although these controls provide some leverage to net out human capital differences, or differences in "merit," we are not controlling for purely objective measures but, rather, subjective evaluations that other research has shown are biased by stereotypic assumptions (Correll et al. 2020;Nelson et al. 2023;Wynn and Correll 2018). In other words, we are controlling for performance and any biases associated with its assessment. As such, our results should be interpreted as conservative estimates of promotion disparities between different gender and race groups. 

To check robustness, we ran all models without controls.

2) 训练与校准（rater 与过程）
- 针对宽严倾向与集中趋势开展系统培训，建立锚定与极端值使用的校准机制；研究指出此类偏差源于主观性与知识不足，可通过培训与流程改变缓解（Okoh 等；51080b06-0）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Leniency or strictness… due to subjectiveness of man… error can be minimized by proper training of managers on appraisal techniques</cite><cite id="51080b06-0">Central tendency… caused by lack of adequate knowledge… can be minimized by training? No—authors emphasize the need to avoid errors but note training is advised for leniency/strictness</cite>.
- 打破社会影响链路：在特定情境下延迟或隔离自我评价，以减少由自我评价引发的群体性偏差（Bohn 等，2023）。<cite id="662f9398-2">Keeping self-evaluations from managers… disrupted social influence… closed the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year</cite>.

3) 数据与机制监控
- 在晋升与薪酬模型中加入对“评级偏差-结果”关系的监控，比如按绩效分位点观察晋升比例与薪酬增幅的斜率是否异质化；若在控制绩效后仍存系统差距，则需重新校准评价权重或引入纠偏项（Castilla, 2008；Correll 等，2020；662f9398-4）。<cite id="662f9398-4">Conservative estimates of promotion disparities show persistent gaps after controlling for performance ratings and tenure</cite>.
- 对比不同业务域、时间序列与绩效水平下的评价分布，识别压缩评分与宽严周期（Prendergast, 1999；Bol 等，2011；51080b06-4）；引入绩效-奖励的弹性映射（banding），以降低极端评级的道德风险。<cite id="51080b06-4">Leniency and centrality biases are frequently observed patterns; leniency inflates rewards, centrality compresses ratings</cite>.

边界与权衡
- 部分偏差具有情境理性：在信息不全与风险规避驱动下，管理者可能有动机压缩评价并维持内部公平，这使得纠偏措施需在效率与公平之间反复权衡（Ittner 等，2003；Moers，2005；Van der Stede 等，2006；51080b06-4）。<cite id="51080b06-4">Subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors, suggesting that assessments are biased; from a superior's perspective, biased rewards may be situationally rational</cite>.
- 并非所有误差均可根除：光环误差等核心认知偏差在提升区分度的同时可能降低信度，且跨群体表现差异可能随任务情境与信息累积而变化，因此治理宜采用组合策略而非单一手段（Frederiksen 等，2017；O’Neill 等，2015；662f9398-1）。<cite id="51080b06-1">No appraisal instrument… satisfactorily resistant to halo error… reducing halo may reduce reliability</cite><cite id="662f9398-1">Bias and halo error remain intractable; performance and expectations jointly shape evaluations</cite>.

实践启示
- 设计上：将关键绩效维度行为化、证据化，采用多源评价与去标识化评审（去除可能引发身份偏差的信息）结合；在奖励模型中使用区间映射而非绝对点数，以降低噪声与中心化扭曲（Bol 等，2016；Bohnen 等，2021；662f9398-3）。<cite id="51080b06-3">Variance components include idiosyncratic rater components across ratee and dimension; unexplained variance underscores design needs</cite><cite id="662f9398-3">Dichotomization reduces racial discrimination in evaluations by discouraging expression of modern racist beliefs</cite>.
- 执行上：强制使用评分表、定期进行评分校准会议、公开行为证据、并开展针对宽严与光环偏差的反思训练；在晋升环节引入交叉评审与申诉机制，以对冲身份与印象偏差（51080b06-0；51080b06-1；662f9398-2）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Proper training on appraisal techniques can minimize leniency/strictness; errors like halo, leniency/strictness, central tendency are well-documented</cite><cite id="51080b06-1">Rater agreement is no guarantee of accuracy; bias and halo error remain intractable</cite><cite id="662f9398-2">Racial and gender gaps in manager ratings lead to the lowest final ratings for women of color; withholding self-evaluations narrows the gap</cite>.

总结
- “绩效错觉转移”可视为由测量噪声与系统偏差共同作用的评价失真现象，其微观机制包括光环/对比、宽严/集中趋势等认知偏差，宏观表现则为种族、性别与民族等社会身份导致的结构性评价差异；这些偏差在组织决策中会扭曲晋升与薪酬，降低激励与公平。治理需在制度设计（行为锚、去标识化、二值化标尺）、过程控制（培训、校准、社会影响隔离）与数据监控（绩效-结果一致性检验）之间建立闭环，同时正视情境理性与核心偏差的不可完全消除性（51080b06-0；51080b06-1；662f9398-0；662f9398-4）。<cite id="51080b06-0">Performance appraisal is frequently subject to many human errors including halo, leniency/strictness, central tendency</cite><cite id="51080b06-1">Bias and halo error are fundamental sources of rater variance; people tend to rate people like themselves more favorably</cite><cite id="662f9398-0">Evaluations appear biased by social identities such as gender, race, or nationality</cite><cite id="662f9398-4">Promotion disparities persist after controlling for performance ratings, indicating biased assessments affect outcomes</cite>.</answer>

Title: Appraisal system: A tool for performance in selected organizations in Nigeria
Snippet: Performance appraisal as a human endeavour is frequently subject to many human errors, although some methods are more prone to errors than others. There are some errors to guard against in rating and other techniques (Baron, 1988;Larson, 1989;Krein, 1990;Okoh, 1998). 

1. Halo effect: In this case, the judgment of raters is influenced by any particularly strong or weak characteristics of the subordinate. This causes the rater to take a generally favourable or unfavourable view of the subordinates other qualities. To reduce the halo effect, the rater, should 1udge all subordinates in one characteristic before going to the next characteristics and so on. 2. Leniency or strictness: This is the tendency of some assessors to be too liberal in their rating by consistently awarding high scores to their subordinates in all job characteristics. On the other hand, some raters also have the tendency to give consistently low scores to their employees. This error is due to the subjectiveness of man. The error can be minimized by proper training of managers on appraisal techniques. If not properly checked, it is capable of setting two departments at loggerheads i.e. a department with a high rater and a department with a low rater manager. 3. Central tendency: Many managers are often unwilling to use the extreme ratings and therefore settle with what is known as the central tendency. This tendency is caused by lack of adequate knowledge of the employees. Since it is obligatory that he must rate his employees, he plays it safe by neither condemning nor praising. If he rates too high or low, he might be required to defend his judgement before top management. So, he takes a central position and rates employees averagely. 4. Matthew effect: Gabris and Mitchell (1989) have reported a disruptive bias in performance appraisal known as the Matthew Effect. It is named after the Matthew of biblical fame who wrote, "To him who has shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him who does not have, even that which he has shall be taken away." In performance appraisal the Matthew Effect is said to occur where employees tend to keep receiving the same appraisal results, year in and year out.

"less effective" managers value consideration, tact, cooperation, teamwork, and loyalty . 9In the same way, raters are differentially accurate in identifying "correct" and "incorrect" job behaviors. 10Even when raters focus on a single behavior or trait, subjectivity breeds variance .Halo error is committed by raters relying on a summary impression of each ratee rather than distinguishing among the levels of performance that individuals exhibit on different job dimensions.Evaluation of any one dimension is not synonymous with performance appraisal as a whole. 12 number of reports conclude that no appraisal instrument or amount of education or experience is satisfactorily resistant to halo error. 13Training sessions in which participants are urged not to commit this error run two related risks.One is that individual raters are not capable of accurately identifying ratees' strong and weak performance areas."Thus, it is possible that reducing halo may also lead to reduced reliability." 14 The other risk is that "making greater distinctions among different performance categories may lead to a reduction in interrater reliability" as well .

Title: AN EFFECTIVE METHOD OF PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL FOR EMPLOYEE MOTIVATION
Snippet: Despite biases, managers have to avoid errors, too. The frequent error that occurs is the 'halo effect'. This happens, when managers rank employees higher because of the positive appearance, which is not always the truth. It means in effect that, managers tend to rank employees higher because of status, appearance, clothing style, relationship, communication, etc. 

For these reasons, it is crucial to be aware of these errors, in order to avoid these kind of mistakes. These kinds of mistakes fool the perception and the performance appraisal, which leads to unusable results.

Title: Manifestation of idiosyncratic rater effect in employee performance appraisal
Snippet: The other well-documented errors/effects, which are known to impact the variations in performance appraisals such as halo error, proximity error, leniency and severity errors, contrast error, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency error, rater attitudes, personal bias and values discrimination between inside and outside employees, employee appearance, etc. (Javidmehr & Ebrahimpour, 2015), are also reasons that contribute towards the idiosyncratic bias of the raters on the performance appraisal of the candidates. Scullen, Mount, and Judge (2003) described the manifestations of rater effect by way of biases such as halo and leniency that have received widespread attention of the researchers in recent times compared to other cognitive biases. Halo error refers to the tendency of raters to allow an overall impression of a ratee to influence judgments along several quasi-independent dimensions (King, Hunter, & Schmidt, 1980), and leniency error is the rater's tendency to assign ratings that are generally either higher or lower than are acceptable by the ratees' actual performance. Hoffman, Lance, Bynum, and Gentry (2010) described idiosyncratic rater bias as a systematic effect that is common only to an individual rater but refrained from offering specifics. O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015) identified the variance components in performance ratings based on generalizability theory (Cronbach et al., 1972), broadly classified the performance ratings' variances two discrete categories, i.e., idiosyncratic rater components and interrater-reliable components. The idiosyncratic rater components were further classified into four-folded rater-related variances identified by O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015): 

1) variances due to rating differences concerning individual rater irrespective of the ratee or the dimension; 2) rating differences on a particular dimension, regardless of the ratee; 3) rating differences on a particular ratee, regardless of the dimension; and 4) unexplained variance. 

Despite having large literature on the idiosyncratic rater effect, the business world appears to be completely unaware of it.

Title: The psychological effects of centrality bias: an experimental analysis
Snippet: The objective of this paper is to advance our knowledge on the behavioural implications of centrality bias. For this reason, we illuminate the psychological mechanisms that are activated by compressed subjective performance evaluations. Subjectivity in the context of performance evaluation has gained considerable momentum in recent years due to the shortcomings of objective performance measures (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011;Cheng and Coyte 2014;Voußem et al. 2016). In particular, objective measures may be insensitive to employees' actions, incongruent with organizational objectives, noisy concerning uncontrollable factors or incomplete with regard to an employee's performance (Bol 2008;Rajan and Reichelstein 2006;Woods 2012). Subjective adjustments to objective performance measures made by the superior during the determination of monetary rewards may mitigate these shortcomings (Dai et al. 2018;Höppe and Moers 2011). 1 Correspondingly, empirical evidence suggests that monetary rewards which are based on subjective assessments have a positive impact on pay satisfaction, productivity and profitability (Gibbs et al. 2004). 

However, a potential drawback of subjective performance evaluation is its inherent discretion (Ittner et al. 2003;Moers 2005;Van der Stede et al. 2006). Prior research indicates that subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011), suggesting that performance assessments by superiors are biased. In this context, leniency bias and centrality bias are two frequently observed patterns (Bol 2011;Frederiksen et al. 2017;Moers 2005;Prendergast 1999). 2 Leniency bias is the tendency to inflate performance rewards, whereas centrality bias leads to compressed ratings. As the result of the latter, the variance in the ratings by the superior is lower than the variance in the performance of the evaluated employees (Bol 2008;Golman and Bhatia 2012). In other words, performers below (above) the average receive a higher (lower) reward than they are actually entitled to according to their performance (Bol et al. 2016). From a superior's perspective, it may be situationally rational to provide biased rewards.

The objective of this paper is to advance our knowledge on the behavioural implications of centrality bias. For this reason, we illuminate the psychological mechanisms that are activated by compressed subjective performance evaluations. Subjectivity in the context of performance evaluation has gained considerable momentum in recent years due to the shortcomings of objective performance measures (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011;Cheng and Coyte 2014;Voußem et al. 2016). In particular, objective measures may be insensitive to employees' actions, incongruent with organizational objectives, noisy concerning uncontrollable factors or incomplete with regard to an employee's performance (Bol 2008;Rajan and Reichelstein 2006;Woods 2012). Subjective adjustments to objective performance measures made by the superior during the determination of monetary rewards may mitigate these shortcomings (Dai et al. 2018;Höppe and Moers 2011). 1 Correspondingly, empirical evidence suggests that monetary rewards which are based on subjective assessments have a positive impact on pay satisfaction, productivity and profitability (Gibbs et al. 2004). 

However, a potential drawback of subjective performance evaluation is its inherent discretion (Ittner et al. 2003;Moers 2005;Van der Stede et al. 2006). Prior research indicates that subjective performance evaluation often implies inaccuracies due to systematic measurement errors (Ahn et al. 2010;Bol 2011), suggesting that performance assessments by superiors are biased. As the result of the latter, the variance in the ratings by the superior is lower than the variance in the performance of the evaluated employees (Bol 2008;Golman and Bhatia 2012). In other words, performers below (above) the average receive a higher (lower) reward than they are actually entitled to according to their performance (Bol et al. 2016). From a superior's perspective, it may be situationally rational to provide biased rewards.

Performance appraisal as a human endeavour is frequently subject to many human errors, although some methods are more prone to errors than others. There are some errors to guard against in rating and other techniques (Baron, 1988;Larson, 1989;Krein, 1990;Okoh, 1998). 

1. Halo effect: In this case, the judgment of raters is influenced by any particularly strong or weak characteristics of the subordinate. This causes the rater to take a generally favourable or unfavourable view of the subordinates other qualities. To reduce the halo effect, the rater, should 1udge all subordinates in one characteristic before going to the next characteristics and so on. 2. Leniency or strictness: This is the tendency of some assessors to be too liberal in their rating by consistently awarding high scores to their subordinates in all job characteristics. On the other hand, some raters also have the tendency to give consistently low scores to their employees. This error is due to the subjectiveness of man. The error can be minimized by proper training of managers on appraisal techniques. If not properly checked, it is capable of setting two departments at loggerheads i.e. a department with a high rater and a department with a low rater manager. 3. Central tendency: Many managers are often unwilling to use the extreme ratings and therefore settle with what is known as the central tendency. This tendency is caused by lack of adequate knowledge of the employees. Since it is obligatory that he must rate his employees, he plays it safe by neither condemning nor praising. If he rates too high or low, he might be required to defend his judgement before top management. So, he takes a central position and rates employees averagely. 4. Matthew effect: Gabris and Mitchell (1989) have reported a disruptive bias in performance appraisal known as the Matthew Effect. It is named after the Matthew of biblical fame who wrote, "To him who has shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him who does not have, even that which he has shall be taken away." In performance appraisal the Matthew Effect is said to occur where employees tend to keep receiving the same appraisal results, year in and year out.

Snippet: Various professions must engage in evaluations of individual behaviours: Legal judges evaluate defendants' actions, teachers grade students' work, personnel managers evaluate applications and conduct performance reviews, and sports judges assess athletes' competitive performance. All such evaluators are expected to assess others impartially and independent of personal characteristics, such as gender, race or nationality. Yet people's assessments of others appear inherently biased, whether consciously or unconsciously, by the social identities of the parties involved. In(ter)group bias "generally refers to the systematic tendency to evaluate one's own membership group (the ingroup) or its members more favourably than a nonmembership group (the outgroup) or its members" (Hewstone et al., 2002, p. 576). In-group favouritism and discriminatory attitudes toward out-group members relate closely, leading to inequity in legal decisions, pay policies, and career chances -as well as championship titles. Understanding the existence and sources of in-group bias or out-group discrimination is critically important to be able to detect, reduce and mitigate the effects of, or even prevent such illegitimate judgments. 

Biased assessments often are based on attributes such as race (Parsons et al., 2011;Price and Wolfers, 2010), gender (Blau and Kahn, 2003) or nationality (Emerson et al., 2009). These attributes can be observed easily and therefore serve as primary research objects for biased judgements. In general, people favour others of the same gender, race or nationality, as confirmed in substantial research that consistently illustrates evaluators' preferences for people from the same country (or race or gender) over non-nationals (or other races or the opposite sex) (see e.g., Ahmed, 2013;Dee, 2005;Emerson et al., 2009;Zitzewitz, 2006). 

In particular, extensive social science research investigates sources of out-group discrimination, revealing that both individual-and contextual-level factors affect discriminatory attitudes and ethnic prejudices. Age is one such variable; in general, younger people express less negative attitudes toward immigrants or people of ethnicities other than their own (see e.g., O'Rourke and Sinnott, 2006;Quillian, 1995).

Title: Expectation vs. reality: How stereotypes and expectation disconfirmation affect job evaluations in online labor markets
Snippet: Another line of research investigated whether the emergence of bias is contingent on the performance of workers. In an experimental study, Jahanbakhsh et al. [7] found that high-performing men and women were evaluated equally. However, when work performance was low, women were rated more unfavorably than men. Greenwood et al. [6] delivered corroborating evidence from an experiment in which female drivers of a fictitious ridesharing app were disproportionately penalized only when quality was low. Conversely, when quality was high, gender did not have an impact on ratings. In contrast, Thebault-Spieker et al. [35] also varied the performance of workers in a series of four experiments but did not find gender bias in any setting. Their analyses suggest that if male and female workers were rated differently, the effect would be lower than 0.2 stars. 

Beyond static conceptions of stereotyping and bias, other work has explored how gender discrimination evolves over time and with accumulating information. Bohren et al. [36] developed a theoretical framework and conducted a field experiment in an online mathematics Q&A forum, showing that women initially face discrimination in evaluations. However, this bias reverses once performance histories accumulate. Over time, women are favored over men with equivalent evaluation records, a pattern that is interpreted as evidence of biased beliefs rather than preference-based discrimination. These findings inform our own investigation by highlighting the critical role of expectations in shaping evaluations. 

To conclude, prior work on gender bias in workers' reputations comes to somewhat conflicting results but points out important moderating factors. Specifically, it seems that bias is evoked when workers' gender does not match the stereotypes associated with a domain or job. Further, bias can be amplified or mitigated, depending on the level of performance. However, none of the aforementioned studies examined the joint influence of both job domain and performance on evaluations (see Fig 1). In the next chapter, we will build upon these findings by considering both factors to derive our hypotheses.

Title: Can gender and race dynamics in performance appraisals be disrupted? The case of social influence
Snippet: Managers’ subjective appraisals of their employees’ performance and employees’ selfevaluations might be affected by demographic characteristics. As self-evaluations are typically shared with managers before they rate employees, social influence may contribute to gender or race differences in performance ratings. Analyzing data from a multi-national firm, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings. We evaluate a quasi-exogenous shock leading to self-evaluations being kept from managers before they appraised employees. This intervention disrupted social influence to some degree, lowering manager ratings and closing the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year of employment. It did not change overall gender or race dynamics. Race dynamics were particularly pronounced in the US where 22-28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would have to be increased for this race gap to disappear. *Bohnet: Harvard Kennedy School, Cambridge, MA, USA. Title: Scale dichotomization reduces customer racial discrimination and income inequality
Snippet: Evaluators may associate racial minorities with negative stereotypes 13 , have implicit biases about minorities [14][15][16] , or hold racial minorities to a higher standard of evaluation [17][18][19] , each of which may lead to lower performance ratings for racial minority workers compared with similar white workers. 

Current interventions to mitigate race-based disparities in organizational contexts, however, focus primarily on improving policies and strategies in selection and recruitment, as well as on implicit bias training 2,3 . It is not feasible to implement such approaches to reduce discrimination by customers in online labour markets, however, and the effectiveness of some common strategies is questionable 3,20 . Furthermore, other potential interventions, such as removing a worker's identifying information, are less suitable for labour markets in which the customer interacts with the worker in person, which requires them to know the worker's identity for safety purposes. 

We examine a potential structural solution [21][22][23] to reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers, specifically, switching from the widely used five-star rating scale to a dichotomous (for example, thumbs up or thumbs down) scale. Reducing the number of scale points seems promising; research has shown that shifting from a ten-point to a six-point rating scale lessened the extent of student discrimination against female professors in the fields of science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Researchers proposed that the change was effective because the number 10 evokes the idea of 'intellectual brilliance', a key notion in academia, which in turn activated gender stereotypes about performance, whereas the number 6 does not elicit these associations 24 . Building on this scale-intervention methodology and sociological research about the role of evaluation structures on observed bias 7,19,24,25 , we propose that dichotomization of the scale used, and not simply reducing the number of scale points, will reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers. We reason that this is because dichotomous scales discourage the expression of modern racist beliefs that manifest as subtle discrimination. 

Psychologists have shown that contemporary forms of racism are often less overt or outwardly hostile than historical forms [26][27][28][29] .

Title: Glass Ceilings, Step Stools, and Sticky Floors: The Racialized Gendered Promotion Process
Snippet: Before combining Black, Latinx, Native, and Pacific Islander men into a single category and Black, Latinx, Native, and Pacific Islander women into another, we tested differences in promotion for men and for women in each of these racial or ethnic groups separately. As mentioned previously, combining these groups into one category allowed us to analyze rather than ignore the experiences of workers in very underrepresented race and gender groups. We decided to combine these groups both because the small numbers in each group limited our ability to estimate separate coefficients for each group at most job levels and because although the content of stereotypes varies, past literature suggests each group faces expectations of lower competence and for women, intersectional invisibility,  which made our hypotheses consistent across each group (Burkley et al. 2017;Ghavami and Peplau 2013;Lee and Fiske 2006). 5  All models control for tenure in position (in years) and performance ratings from the prior year. We control for tenure in position because we expect that the longer a worker is in a given job, the more likely it is the worker will be promoted. To estimate tenure in position for individuals in 2013 (the first year of data), we rely on last promotion date and start date data provided by TECH INC. Performance ratings are measured on a continuous numeric 9-point scale. The lowest value is equivalent to a "lowest performing," evaluation and the highest value is equivalent to a "highest performing" evaluation. Managers assess workers' performance regularly and log ratings in personnel systems. Managers are advised to make promotion recommendations based on performance ratings, consistent with meritbased models at many companies (e.g., Castilla 2008;Correll et al. 2020). Although these controls provide some leverage to net out human capital differences, or differences in "merit," we are not controlling for purely objective measures but, rather, subjective evaluations that other research has shown are biased by stereotypic assumptions (Correll et al. 2020;Nelson et al. 2023;Wynn and Correll 2018). In other words, we are controlling for performance and any biases associated with its assessment. As such, our results should be interpreted as conservative estimates of promotion disparities between different gender and race groups. 

To check robustness, we ran all models without controls.

We decided to combine these groups both because the small numbers in each group limited our ability to estimate separate coefficients for each group at most job levels and because although the content of stereotypes varies, past literature suggests each group faces expectations of lower competence and for women, intersectional invisibility,  which made our hypotheses consistent across each group (Burkley et al. 2017;Ghavami and Peplau 2013;Lee and Fiske 2006). 5  All models control for tenure in position (in years) and performance ratings from the prior year. We control for tenure in position because we expect that the longer a worker is in a given job, the more likely it is the worker will be promoted. To estimate tenure in position for individuals in 2013 (the first year of data), we rely on last promotion date and start date data provided by TECH INC. Performance ratings are measured on a continuous numeric 9-point scale. The lowest value is equivalent to a "lowest performing," evaluation and the highest value is equivalent to a "highest performing" evaluation. Managers assess workers' performance regularly and log ratings in personnel systems. documents.title: The Impact of Age on Nationality Bias: Evidence from Ski Jumping
documents.snippet:
Various professions must engage in evaluations of individual behaviours: Legal judges evaluate defendants' actions, teachers grade students' work, personnel managers evaluate applications and conduct performance reviews, and sports judges assess athletes' competitive performance. All such evaluators are expected to assess others impartially and independent of personal characteristics, such as gender, race or nationality. Yet people's assessments of others appear inherently biased, whether consciously or unconsciously, by the social identities of the parties involved. In(ter)group bias "generally refers to the systematic tendency to evaluate one's own membership group (the ingroup) or its members more favourably than a nonmembership group (the outgroup) or its members" (Hewstone et al., 2002, p. 576). In-group favouritism and discriminatory attitudes toward out-group members relate closely, leading to inequity in legal decisions, pay policies, and career chances -as well as championship titles. Understanding the existence and sources of in-group bias or out-group discrimination is critically important to be able to detect, reduce and mitigate the effects of, or even prevent such illegitimate judgments. 

Biased assessments often are based on attributes such as race (Parsons et al., 2011;Price and Wolfers, 2010), gender (Blau and Kahn, 2003) or nationality (Emerson et al., 2009). These attributes can be observed easily and therefore serve as primary research objects for biased judgements. In general, people favour others of the same gender, race or nationality, as confirmed in substantial research that consistently illustrates evaluators' preferences for people from the same country (or race or gender) over non-nationals (or other races or the opposite sex) (see e.g., Ahmed, 2013;Dee, 2005;Emerson et al., 2009;Zitzewitz, 2006). 

In particular, extensive social science research investigates sources of out-group discrimination, revealing that both individual-and contextual-level factors affect discriminatory attitudes and ethnic prejudices. Age is one such variable; in general, younger people express less negative attitudes toward immigrants or people of ethnicities other than their own (see e.g., O'Rourke and Sinnott, 2006;Quillian, 1995).

documents.title: Expectation vs. reality: How stereotypes and expectation disconfirmation affect job evaluations in online labor markets
documents.snippet:
Another line of research investigated whether the emergence of bias is contingent on the performance of workers. In an experimental study, Jahanbakhsh et al. [7] found that high-performing men and women were evaluated equally. However, when work performance was low, women were rated more unfavorably than men. Greenwood et al. [6] delivered corroborating evidence from an experiment in which female drivers of a fictitious ridesharing app were disproportionately penalized only when quality was low. Conversely, when quality was high, gender did not have an impact on ratings. In contrast, Thebault-Spieker et al. [35] also varied the performance of workers in a series of four experiments but did not find gender bias in any setting. Their analyses suggest that if male and female workers were rated differently, the effect would be lower than 0.2 stars. 

Beyond static conceptions of stereotyping and bias, other work has explored how gender discrimination evolves over time and with accumulating information. Bohren et al. [36] developed a theoretical framework and conducted a field experiment in an online mathematics Q&A forum, showing that women initially face discrimination in evaluations. However, this bias reverses once performance histories accumulate. Over time, women are favored over men with equivalent evaluation records, a pattern that is interpreted as evidence of biased beliefs rather than preference-based discrimination. These findings inform our own investigation by highlighting the critical role of expectations in shaping evaluations. 

To conclude, prior work on gender bias in workers' reputations comes to somewhat conflicting results but points out important moderating factors. Specifically, it seems that bias is evoked when workers' gender does not match the stereotypes associated with a domain or job. Further, bias can be amplified or mitigated, depending on the level of performance. However, none of the aforementioned studies examined the joint influence of both job domain and performance on evaluations (see Fig 1). In the next chapter, we will build upon these findings by considering both factors to derive our hypotheses.

documents.title: Can gender and race dynamics in performance appraisals be disrupted? The case of social influence
documents.snippet: Managers’ subjective appraisals of their employees’ performance and employees’ selfevaluations might be affected by demographic characteristics. As self-evaluations are typically shared with managers before they rate employees, social influence may contribute to gender or race differences in performance ratings. Analyzing data from a multi-national firm, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings. We evaluate a quasi-exogenous shock leading to self-evaluations being kept from managers before they appraised employees. This intervention disrupted social influence to some degree, lowering manager ratings and closing the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year of employment. It did not change overall gender or race dynamics. Race dynamics were particularly pronounced in the US where 22-28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would have to be increased for this race gap to disappear. *Bohnet: Harvard Kennedy School, Cambridge, MA, USA. documents.title: Scale dichotomization reduces customer racial discrimination and income inequality
documents.snippet:
Evaluators may associate racial minorities with negative stereotypes 13 , have implicit biases about minorities [14][15][16] , or hold racial minorities to a higher standard of evaluation [17][18][19] , each of which may lead to lower performance ratings for racial minority workers compared with similar white workers. 

Current interventions to mitigate race-based disparities in organizational contexts, however, focus primarily on improving policies and strategies in selection and recruitment, as well as on implicit bias training 2,3 . It is not feasible to implement such approaches to reduce discrimination by customers in online labour markets, however, and the effectiveness of some common strategies is questionable 3,20 . Furthermore, other potential interventions, such as removing a worker's identifying information, are less suitable for labour markets in which the customer interacts with the worker in person, which requires them to know the worker's identity for safety purposes. 

We examine a potential structural solution [21][22][23] to reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers, specifically, switching from the widely used five-star rating scale to a dichotomous (for example, thumbs up or thumbs down) scale. Reducing the number of scale points seems promising; research has shown that shifting from a ten-point to a six-point rating scale lessened the extent of student discrimination against female professors in the fields of science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Researchers proposed that the change was effective because the number 10 evokes the idea of 'intellectual brilliance', a key notion in academia, which in turn activated gender stereotypes about performance, whereas the number 6 does not elicit these associations 24 . Building on this scale-intervention methodology and sociological research about the role of evaluation structures on observed bias 7,19,24,25 , we propose that dichotomization of the scale used, and not simply reducing the number of scale points, will reduce racial discrimination in customer evaluations of workers. We reason that this is because dichotomous scales discourage the expression of modern racist beliefs that manifest as subtle discrimination. 

Psychologists have shown that contemporary forms of racism are often less overt or outwardly hostile than historical forms [26][27][28][29] .
